nodes.l3: Variolation is documented in Asia and Africa before Jenner. The eradication of smallpox is documented by the World Health Organization, and long-run mortality series show the effect of each vaccination programme directly.
nodes.ev: Historical inoculation records; eradication documentation; mortality series

nodes.date: 1928 CE onward; clinical from 1942
nodes.l1: Chemicals that kill bacteria without killing you.
nodes.l2: Before antibiotics, a scratch could be fatal and most surgery carried a serious infection risk. Their arrival changed medicine so completely that the pre-antibiotic world is hard to imagine. Resistance was predicted by Fleming himself in his Nobel lecture, and it is now a serious and growing problem.
nodes.l3: Fleming's 1928 observation, the Oxford team's clinical development in the 1940s, and subsequent resistance surveillance are all documented. Resistance rates are tracked by national and international monitoring programmes.
nodes.ev: Original research records; clinical trial history; resistance surveillance
nodes.caution: Antibiotic resistance is rising and was anticipated from the beginning. This is a gain that is not guaranteed to persist.

nodes.date: ≈ 1907 CE onward
nodes.l1: Long molecular chains that can be shaped into almost anything.
nodes.l2: Plastics can be made light, strong, flexible, insulating, transparent or sterile as required, and cheaply. They made modern medicine, electronics and food safety possible in their present form. The same durability that makes them useful means they persist in the environment for a very long time, and that consequence took decades to register.
nodes.l3: Bakelite's 1907 synthesis and subsequent polymer chemistry are documented in patents and the research literature. Production statistics and environmental monitoring — including microplastic distribution studies — document the scale.
nodes.ev: Polymer patents and literature; production statistics; environmental monitoring
nodes.caution: Plastics' durability is both their advantage and their environmental problem. Both belong in any honest account.

nodes.date: Purified at scale from the 1950s
nodes.l1: Sand, purified to roughly one impure atom in a billion.
nodes.l2: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust and utterly useless for electronics in its natural state. What made the semiconductor industry possible was purification and crystal growth — producing single crystals of a perfection unmatched by any other bulk manufactured material. The scarcity was never the element; it was the process.
nodes.l3: The Czochralski crystal-growth process, zone refining and semiconductor-grade purity specifications are documented in the materials science literature and in industrial standards.
nodes.ev: Crystal growth literature; purity specifications; industry standards

nodes.date: ≈ 1935 CE onward
nodes.l1: Finding things by bouncing radio waves off them and timing the echo.
nodes.l2: Radar gave sight through darkness, cloud and distance. Its development drove microwave electronics hard — the cavity magnetron in particular — and that wartime push fed directly into post-war electronics, radio astronomy and, eventually, the microwave oven, which is a rather blunt illustration of dual-use technology.
nodes.l3: Development records, surviving equipment and IEEE milestone documentation record the systems and their performance. The technology transfer into civilian electronics is well traced.
nodes.ev: Development records; surviving equipment; IEEE milestones

nodes.date: 1957 CE onward
nodes.l1: A machine placed in orbit, falling around the Earth indefinitely.
nodes.l2: Orbit gives a vantage point over a whole hemisphere at once, which is why satellites transformed communication, weather forecasting, navigation, mapping and climate monitoring simultaneously. Most of what is known about global climate change comes from instruments that had to be put above the atmosphere to work.
nodes.l3: Launch records, orbital catalogues and the continuous data archives from Earth observation missions are public. Satellite counts and launch-cost series are tracked over decades.
nodes.ev: Launch and orbital records; Earth observation data archives

nodes.date: Fully operational 1995 CE
nodes.l1: Knowing exactly where you are, anywhere, from timing signals in space.
nodes.l2: Position is computed from the tiny differences in arrival time of signals from several satellites — which means the system depends on clocks accurate to nanoseconds, and on correcting for relativistic time dilation. Without applying both special and general relativity, positions would drift by kilometres per day. It is the most routine practical use of Einstein's physics there is.
nodes.l3: System specifications, published accuracy analyses and the documented relativistic corrections are public. Independent verification of the relativistic effects is a standard textbook case.
nodes.ev: System specifications; accuracy analyses; relativistic correction documentation

nodes.date: ≈ 5,000 years ago onward, earliest in Egypt and Mesopotamia
nodes.l1: A unit of weight that means the same thing in every market.
nodes.l2: Trade beyond a small circle of trust needs a shared standard, not just mutual goodwill — a trader from one city has to be able to check a merchant's weights against a known reference. States backed this with enforcement: inspected weight sets, stamped denominations, and penalties for short-weighting. Once weight and length are standardized, price comparison, taxation and large contracts between strangers all become practical.
nodes.l3: Sets of stone and bronze weights, calibrated against each other and often stamped with a denomination, survive by the thousands from Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and the Aegean. Comparing weight sets across sites is how archaeologists reconstruct which regions shared a trading standard.
nodes.ev: Calibrated weight sets; stamped denominations; cross-site weight comparisons

nodes.date: Temple and merchant lending ≈ 4,000 years ago onward; formal banks from medieval Italy
nodes.l1: Other people's money, held, lent and tracked by a third party.
nodes.l2: Banking separates saving from spending: a deposit can be lent to someone else while the depositor still expects it back on demand. Mesopotamian temples and merchant houses acted as lenders and safekeepers millennia before anything called a 'bank' existed; what changed in medieval Italy was formalizing the ledger, the interest calculation and the cross-city transfer into a specialised trade of its own.
nodes.l3: Cuneiform loan contracts record interest rates, collateral and repayment terms from the early second millennium BCE. Medieval Italian merchant-bank account books are the direct ancestor of the modern bank statement.
nodes.ev: Cuneiform loan contracts; medieval Italian merchant-bank ledgers

nodes.date: Formalised in print by Luca Pacioli, 1494 (Venice); practised earlier by Italian merchants
nodes.l1: Every transaction recorded twice, so the books have to balance.
nodes.l2: Double-entry turns bookkeeping into a self-checking system: each transaction is entered as a debit in one account and a matching credit in another, so total debits must equal total credits. An error throws the books out of balance and announces itself — exactly what a merchant running several ventures at once needs, and what let businesses grow past the size one person could track from memory.
nodes.l3: Luca Pacioli's 1494 Summa de arithmetica did not invent the method — Venetian and Genoese merchants were already using it — but his printed description is the earliest surviving full account of the technique, and print is what spread the practice across Europe.
nodes.ev: Pacioli's Summa de arithmetica (1494); earlier Italian merchant ledgers

nodes.date: Incense and Silk Road networks active from ≈ 2,000–3,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Goods carried overland across a distance no single trader ever walks start to finish.
nodes.l2: A caravan route is a relay, not one journey — goods, and the profit taken on them, pass through many hands between source and destination, each leg run by people who know that particular stretch of road. Silk moved west and glass moved east along the same corridors that also carried papermaking, religious ideas and disease.
nodes.l3: Way-station and caravanserai remains, incense-route forts and wells in Arabia, and Silk Road oasis cities mark the infrastructure that made the relay possible, and let historians reconstruct route capacity and timing.
nodes.ev: Way-station and caravanserai forts; oasis city excavations

nodes.date: ≈ 500,000 years ago or earlier (debated)
nodes.l1: A stone blade secured to a wooden handle. More effective than either alone.
nodes.l2: Hafting — attaching a stone head to a wooden shaft — multiplies the utility of both materials. The leverage of the handle amplifies force; the durability of the stone preserves an edge. This combination made hunting, processing, and construction work radically more efficient.
nodes.l3: Evidence of hafted tools appears in the archaeological record by the Middle Pleistocene, with clear examples from Acheulean and Mousterian tool kits. The technique required not just the ability to shape stone and select wood, but to understand how materials with different properties could be joined to complement each other's strengths.
nodes.ev: Archaeological tool assemblages

nodes.l1: Burning material carried on a stick: fire you can take with you.
nodes.l2: A torch turns fire from a place into a tool. It lights the way into caves, keeps animals back at night, and carries a flame from one hearth to start the next.
nodes.l3: Torches rarely survive, so evidence is indirect: soot marks and charcoal smears on cave walls far beyond the reach of daylight.

nodes.l2: A point concentrates the whole swing on a tiny area, which is what hard ground and seamed rock need. Picks made from antler were a standard mining tool long before metal ones.
nodes.l3: Worn antler picks left behind in ancient mine shafts and pits are the usual evidence.

nodes.l2: The handle turns the arm into a longer lever, so each blow lands harder than a hand-held stone could. Felling and shaping timber at scale depends on it.
nodes.l3: Stone axe heads survive well and often show polish or wear where a handle once gripped them; the handles themselves rarely survive.

nodes.l2: An adze takes off thin curls instead of chopping through, which is what shaping a plank, a bowl or a canoe hull requires.
nodes.l3: Archaeologists tell adze blades from axe blades by their asymmetric edge and wear pattern.

nodes.l2: Careful heating drives moisture out of the tip and makes it harder and less likely to split — a sharper weapon with no stone at all.
nodes.l3: Wooden spears are among the rarest survivals in archaeology; where they do survive, waterlogged or buried, their tips can be examined for heat treatment.

nodes.l3: Stone points with damage typical of impact, and with traces of the glue or binding that held them, are the main evidence.

nodes.l2: Barbs and a line let a hunter keep hold of something in water, where a plain spear would simply come loose and be lost.
nodes.l3: Carved bone and antler points with barbs are the typical finds; how early they appear is actively debated.

nodes.l2: Striking the tool instead of swinging it gives precise, controlled cuts — the basis of joinery and carving.

nodes.l2: A bolas does not need to hit a vital spot; it only has to wrap around something moving. It is a way of catching fast animals alive.

nodes.l2: Cleaning a hide is slow, repetitive work, and a scraper's robust edge survives it. Scrapers are among the most common tools in many stone tool assemblages.
nodes.l3: Microscopic wear and residues on scraper edges show what they were used on — hide, wood or plant.

nodes.l2: Cutting wild cereals by the handful is far quicker with a sickle than by hand, which matters once people start relying on grain.

nodes.l2: A hook lets one person fish from a shore or a boat without nets or traps, and it works in deep water where spears cannot reach.
nodes.l3: Hooks carved from shell and bone are among the finds; the oldest examples known come from islands in the western Pacific.

nodes.date: Older than us
nodes.l1: Living plants for food, medicine, fiber, and tools.
nodes.l2: Plants are the foundation of human diet and material culture. Every ecosystem offers edible plants, medicinal plants, and plants for fiber or construction.
nodes.l3: Plant processing gave us fiber, food preservation, medicine, and poisons.

nodes.date: Older than us
nodes.l1: Dried grass and reeds for thatching and bedding.
nodes.l2: Grass provides insulation, water resistance, and structure when dried and bundled together.
nodes.l3: Thatch made from grass and reeds is one of the oldest roofing materials.
nodes.ev: Archaeological remains of thatched structures

nodes.date: ≈ 50,000 years ago or earlier
nodes.l1: Woven or felted fibers forming a flexible material.
nodes.l2: Cloth can be made from plant fibers or animal hair by weaving or felting strands together.
nodes.l3: Early cloth provided protection from weather and later became a medium for decoration and social signaling.

nodes.date: ≈ 10,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Bundled grass or reeds tied together to form weatherproof covering.
nodes.l2: Thatch is a durable roofing material that sheds water and insulates. It can last 30+ years if properly maintained.
nodes.l3: Thatch roofs require specific construction knowledge and are particularly suited to areas with abundant grass or reeds.
nodes.ev: Archaeological remains of thatched structures across multiple continents

nodes.date: ≈ 50,000 years ago or earlier
nodes.l1: Open mesh of knotted cordage for catching fish and small game.
nodes.l2: Nets dramatically increase hunting and fishing efficiency by creating a boundary that animals cannot see or understand. A single net can trap many animals where a spear might catch one.
nodes.l3: Nets appear in the archaeological record as impressions, wear patterns on tools, and in artistic representations. They are older than agriculture and remain one of humanity's most important food-acquisition technologies.
nodes.ev: Net fragments, artistic depictions, tool wear patterns

nodes.date: ≈ 40,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Cordage twisted into thread, sharpened bone shaped into needle.
nodes.l2: Thread and needle enable sewn clothing, which allowed humans to adapt clothing to fit their body precisely, crucial for surviving cold climates.
nodes.l3: Sewn clothing appears in the archaeological record around 40,000 years ago, coinciding with human expansion into colder regions.
nodes.ev: Bone needles, tool marks, sewn fabric fragments

nodes.date: Older than recorded history
nodes.l1: Smoke created by burning bone and fiber to repel insects and animals.
nodes.l2: Smudge fires create dense smoke that repels biting insects and keeps animals at a distance. Critical for survival in warm climates with aggressive insect swarms.
nodes.l3: Smudging remains an important technique for both insect control and ceremonial purposes in many cultures.
nodes.ev: Ash deposits with bone char, ethnographic evidence

nodes.date: ≈ 10,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Thatch made from bundled grass, reeds, or straw, used to cover and insulate roofs.
nodes.l2: Thatched roofs are remarkably durable, shedding water effectively while providing excellent insulation. A well-built thatch roof can last 30-60 years.
nodes.l3: Thatching is a specialized craft requiring knowledge of local materials and building techniques. Thatched structures remain common in regions with abundant grass or reed.
nodes.ev: Archaeological remains of thatched structures, reconstructions

nodes.date: ≈ 50,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Thin cordage made from plant fibers, useful for fine work and delicate applications.
nodes.l2: Plant-derived fibers can be processed into extremely thin, strong threads suitable for sewing fine cloth, making nets with small mesh, and detailed basketry.
nodes.l3: Different plants yield fibers with different properties: flax produces strong fine thread, hemp produces rough strong cordage, and various plants yield specialty fibers.
nodes.ev: Fiber fragments, impressions, artistic depictions

nodes.date: ≈ 10,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Thatch woven into flat, flexible sheets for flooring, walls, or portable shelter.
nodes.l2: Mats provide insulation and waterproofing. They can be rolled up for transport, making them ideal for nomadic peoples. Tightly woven mats can also serve as walls or temporary shelters.
nodes.l3: Mat-weaving remains an important technology in cultures with abundant reed or grass. Mat designs reflect regional plant availability and cultural preferences.
nodes.ev: Mat fragments, impressions in clay, artwork

nodes.date: ≈ 8,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Long fibers extracted from flax plants, processed into strong, fine thread and linen cloth.
nodes.l2: Flax fibers are exceptionally strong and fine, producing the smoothest and strongest plant-derived fabric. Linen made from flax resists rotting and improves with age and washing.
nodes.l3: Flax production requires specialized knowledge: planting, retting (water-soaking), breaking, scutching (beating), and hackling (combing). Ancient Egyptians prized linen for both clothing and mummification wraps.
nodes.ev: Flax seeds, processed fiber, linen cloth fragments, artwork

nodes.date: ≈ 10,000 years ago or earlier
nodes.l1: Wooden trap with net webbing that fish swim into but cannot escape from easily.
nodes.l2: Fish traps are passive fishing technology that allows continuous capture without constant attention. They can be left in place and checked periodically, making fishing more efficient.
nodes.l3: Different fish traps are optimized for different species and water conditions. Some rely on funnel entrances that fish can find but cannot navigate back through.
nodes.ev: Preserved traps, artistic depictions, tool wear patterns

nodes.date: Date not yet sourced
nodes.l1: Net weighted with stones or bone, designed to sink and trap fish and aquatic animals.
nodes.l2: Weighted nets sink to the bottom and can cover a larger area. When deployed strategically in water, they trap fish trying to escape. The Retiarius (net-fighter) of ancient Rome used a similar concept as a weapon.
nodes.l3: Weighted casting nets remain a highly effective fishing technique. A skilled fisher can cast a weighted net and retrieve a catch with a single motion.
nodes.ev: Net weights (stones with grooves), net fragments, artwork

nodes.date: ≈ 3,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Decorated cloth created by stitching thread into existing cloth to form patterns and images.
nodes.l2: Embroidery adds aesthetic value and symbolic meaning to cloth. It transforms plain fabric into art, and in many cultures, embroidery patterns communicate identity, status, and cultural affiliation.
nodes.l3: Different cultures developed distinct embroidery styles. Chinese silk embroidery, Middle Eastern gold thread work, and European needlepoint each represent sophisticated artistic traditions.
nodes.ev: Embroidered textiles, artwork, historical garments

nodes.date: ≈ 2,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Cloth dyed or decorated to blend with natural surroundings for hunting or military purposes.
nodes.l2: Camouflage works by breaking up the visual outline and matching the colors of the environment. Effective camouflage requires understanding local colors, textures, and lighting conditions.
nodes.l3: Modern military camouflage patterns evolved from hunting traditions. Each environment requires different patterns: forest, desert, snow, and urban camouflage all use different color and shape combinations.
nodes.ev: Historical hunting garments, military uniforms, natural dye analysis

nodes.date: ≈ 3,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Plant fibers broken down into a mushy consistency for papermaking or insulation.
nodes.l2: Pulp is created by soaking plant fibers in water and beating them until they break down into fine fibers. This pulp can be spread thin and dried to make paper, or used for insulation and padding.
nodes.l3: Chinese papermaking, developed around 2,000 years ago, refined pulp-making techniques. Quality paper requires controlling fiber length, fiber distribution, and the density of the final sheet.
nodes.ev: Paper fragments, papermaking equipment, historical documents

nodes.date: ≈ 2.6 million years ago onward
nodes.l1: A hand-sized cobble used to strike other stone.
nodes.l2: A hammerstone is a hard, rounded rock held in the hand and used to knock flakes off a core. Battered ends and pitted surfaces are the sign that a cobble was used this way.
nodes.l3: Every stone knapper since has needed one, which makes it one of the longest-running tools in the record.

nodes.l2: Strictly speaking, the earliest Oldowan tools were choppers, cores and flakes; the shaped teardrop handaxe belongs to the later Acheulean. The game groups the earliest heavy-duty cores under this name.
nodes.l3: It marks the step from picking up a lucky sharp rock to deliberately making one.
